lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.unitTitle: Systems of Linear Equations and Inequalities
lessonRef.focus: why elimination is a justified move, not a trick
lessonRef.title: Transfer challenge: why elimination is a justified move, not a trick

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: The example is from a different context than the problems below.

items.prompt: How many solutions has 2x + y = 5 and 4x + 2y = 11?

steps: The lines are parallel and distinct.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: Is the point (-2, 1) in the solution region of 2x + 6y ≤ 2?
choices: Only points on the boundary line are in the solution region.
The region cannot be tested without graphing it first.
No; substituting gives 2, which is greater than 2.

items.prompt: A student replaces the second equation of a system with (second equation) + 2 × (first equation). Which statement is correct?
choices: The new system may lose solutions that the original had.
The new system may gain solutions that the original did not have.
The new system is equivalent only when 2 is 1.
The new system has exactly the same solution set, because the replacement step is reversible.

items.prompt:
How many solutions does this system have?
  2x + 4y = -5
  3x + 4y = -2

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: These are meant to be hard. Show the reasoning even if you do not finish.

items.prompt: Is the point (-6, -5) in the solution region of -1x − 6y ≤ 11?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: A student replaces the second equation of a system with (second equation) + 5 × (first equation). Which statement is correct?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
